extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students and researchers in number theory; readers of mathematical proof-exposition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and meta-criteria for selecting, structuring, and evaluating proofs in elementary number theory (examples: representations as sums of two squares; quadratic reciprocity; finite division-ring arguments). Focuses on proof-ideas, decomposition into lemmas/facts, and choice of methods (combinatorial, algebraic, analytic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for choosing 'Book' proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Which proof belongs in the Book? Is it the shortest, the most unexpected, or should one look for the proof that had the greatest potential for generalizations to other and deeper reciprocity laws?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors state that selection balances simplicity/pleasing form and potential for generalization: they chose two proofs for quadratic reciprocity — one 'simplest and most pleasing' and another that is 'the starting point for fundamental results in more general structures.' Use this as a rubric when deciding which proofs to highlight: brevity, surprise/elegance, and capacity to generalize are positive criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance / Surprise as a quality of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs described as 'elegant and surprising' are given preference; such proofs often employ clever, compact ideas (e.g. Thue's pigeonhole argument, Heath-Brown's involutions, Eisenstein's lattice-point counting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek arguments that reveal an unexpected structure or use a short clever idea (pigeonhole, involutions, lattice counting) rather than lengthy technical machinery. Example: Thue's pigeonhole-based proof that primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) are sums of two squares is characterized as a 'Book Proof' due to its cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructiveness / effectiveness of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between existence proofs and effective/constructive proofs: 'Both proofs are not effective: Try to find x and y for a ten digit prime! Efficient ways to find such representations as sums of two squares are discussed in [references].'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the goal is computation, prefer proofs or methods that yield explicit algorithms (effective methods). Non-constructive proofs establishing existence may be elegant but are insufficient when an explicit representation or algorithm is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decompose major theorems into small, checkable facts/lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem (sum of two squares) is presented as consequence of five facts: base representable cases (1,2, primes p≡1 mod4), closure under product, closure under multiplication by a square, a divisibility property for primes p≡3 mod4, and a reduction step n/p^2 representability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving a structural theorem, break it into elementary, reusable facts (base cases, closure properties, local prime-power analyses, and reduction arguments). The exposition demonstrates how assembling simple facts yields the full theorem; list the facts explicitly and prove them separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of elementary counting / combinatorial principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ combinatorial tools such as the pigeonhole principle and counting lattice points. Example: Thue’s proof uses the pigeonhole principle; Eisenstein’s proof of quadratic reciprocity is 'just counting lattice points.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer proofs that reduce algebraic questions to combinatorial/counting statements when possible; these often yield short, conceptual arguments. Provide the combinatorial setup clearly (domains, counts, contradictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Gauss's lemma / Legendre symbol techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Gauss's lemma (count of negative residues among ia reduced to smallest absolute value) is a fundamental tool for proofs of quadratic reciprocity and for computing Legendre symbols. Euler’s criterion and product rules for Legendre symbols are essential computational tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working with quadratic residues and reciprocity, explicitly apply Gauss's lemma or Euler's criterion and exploit the product rule ( (ab|p) = (a|p)(b|p) ). Use reductions to counting signs or residues to convert multiplicative questions to parity/counting questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of algebraic/field-theoretic methods (Gauss sums, finite fields)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gauss sums and properties of finite fields provide alternative proofs of reciprocity. Example: compute a Gauss sum G in two ways (G^q and G^{(q-1)/2}) and equate to obtain the reciprocity law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For deeper or more structural proofs, set the problem in an appropriate finite field or cyclotomic setting and exploit field automorphisms, characters, and Gauss sums. This approach is well-suited when one needs connections to algebraic number theory or generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight the 'crux' of the argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and emphasize the single crucial observation (the 'crux') of a proof; e.g., 'According to Erdős, this is the crux of the proof' when proving ai’s are the integers 1..k in some order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly point out the pivotal step or lemma that the rest of the argument hinges on, and explain why it resolves the main difficulty. Labelling and isolating the 'crux' helps readers grasp the architecture of the proof and understand what is novel or hard.
